text:
NORA. Tomorrow I am going home— I mean, to my old hometown. It will be easiest for me there to find my way into something or other.

HELMER. Oh, you blind, inexperienced creature.

NORA. I must try to gain experience, Torvald.

HELMER. Leave your home, your husband, and your children! And you do not think about what people will say.

NORA. I cannot take that into consideration. I only know that it will be necessary for me.

HELMER. Oh, it is outrageous. That you can betray your most sacred duties in this way.

NORA. What, then, do you consider my most sacred duties?

HELMER. And should I have to tell you that! Are they not your duties toward your husband and your children?

NORA. I have other, equally sacred duties.

HELMER. You do not. What duties could those be?

NORA. My duties toward myself.

HELMER. First and foremost, you are a wife and mother.

NORA. I no longer believe that. I believe that first and foremost I am a human being, I, just as much as you are—or at any rate that I shall try to become one. I know very well that most people agree with you, Torvald, and that something of the sort is written in the books. But I can no longer content myself with what most people say and what is written in the books. I must think those things over for myself and try to understand them.

HELMER. Should you not understand your position in your own home? Do you not have an infallible guide in such matters? Do you not have religion?

NORA. Oh, Torvald, I really do not properly know what religion is at all.

HELMER. What are you saying!

NORA. I know nothing except what Pastor Hansen said when I was preparing for confirmation. He told us that religion was this and that. When I get away from all this here and am alone, I shall investigate that matter too. I shall see whether what Pastor Hansen said was right, or at any rate whether it is right for me.

HELMER. Oh, such a thing is really unheard of from so young a woman! But if religion cannot guide you, then at least let me stir your conscience. You do have moral feeling, surely? Or answer me—perhaps you have none?

NORA. Well, Torvald, that is not easy to answer. I really do not know at all. I am completely at a loss about those things. I only know that I have an entirely different opinion about such matters from you. I now also hear that the laws are different from what I thought; but that those laws should be right is something I simply cannot get into my head. So a woman is not to have the right to spare her old, dying father, or to save her husband’s life! I do not believe in such things.

HELMER. You speak like a child. You do not understand the society in which you live.

NORA. No, I do not. But now I shall acquaint myself with it. I must try to find out who is right, society or I.

HELMER. You are ill, Nora; you have a fever; I almost think you are out of your senses.

NORA. I have never felt so clear and certain as I do tonight.

HELMER. And clear and certain, you leave your husband and your children?

NORA. Yes; I do.

HELMER. Then only one explanation is possible.

NORA. Which one?

HELMER. You do not love me anymore.

NORA. No, that is precisely it.

HELMER. Nora!—And you say that!

NORA. Oh, it hurts me so much, Torvald; for you have always been so kind to me. But I cannot help it. I do not love you anymore.

HELMER (with hard-won composure). Is this too a clear and certain conviction?

NORA. Yes, perfectly clear and certain. That is why I do not want to be here any longer.

HELMER. And will you also be able to explain to me how I have forfeited your love?

NORA. Yes, I can easily do that. It was this evening, when the wonderful thing did not happen; for then I saw that you were not the man I had imagined you to be.

HELMER. Explain yourself more precisely; I do not understand you.

NORA. I have waited so patiently for eight years now; for, good Lord, I understood well enough that the wonderful thing does not happen like that every day. Then this crushing blow broke over me; and then I was so unshakably certain: now the wonderful thing will happen. When Krogstad’s letter was lying out there, it never entered my mind for an instant that you might be willing to submit to that man’s terms. I was so unshakably certain that you would say to him: make the matter known to the whole world. And when that had happened—

HELMER. Yes, what then? When I had surrendered my own wife to shame and disgrace—!

NORA. When that had happened, I thought with such unshakable certainty that you would step forward, take everything upon yourself, and say: I am the guilty one.

HELMER. Nora—!

NORA. You think that I would never have accepted such a sacrifice from you? No, of course not. But what would my assurances have counted for against yours?—That was the wonderful thing for which I went on hoping in terror. And it was to prevent it that I wanted to end my life.

HELMER. I would gladly work nights and days for you, Nora—bear sorrow and privation for your sake. But no one sacrifices his honor for the one he loves.

NORA. A hundred thousand women have done so.

HELMER. Oh, you both think and speak like an unreasonable child.

NORA. So be it. But you neither think nor speak like the man with whom I could unite myself. When your terror was over—not at what threatened me, but at what you yourself were exposed to—and when all the danger was past, then for you it was as though absolutely nothing had happened. I was exactly as before, your little song-lark, your doll, whom you would henceforth carry doubly carefully in your hands, since it was so fragile and frail. (Rises.) Torvald—in that moment it dawned on me that for eight years I had lived here with a strange man, and that I had borne three children—. Oh, I cannot bear to think of it! I could tear myself into bits and pieces.

HELMER (heavily). I see it; I see it. An abyss has surely opened between us.—Oh, but Nora, could it not be filled in?

NORA. As I am now, I am no wife for you.

HELMER. I have the strength to become another man.

NORA. Perhaps—if your doll is taken away from you.

HELMER. Oh, to part—to part from you! No, no, Nora, I cannot grasp that thought.

NORA (goes into the room on the right). All the more certainly must it happen. (She returns with her outer garments and a small traveling bag, which she places on the chair by the table.)

HELMER. Nora, Nora, not now! Wait until tomorrow.

NORA (puts on her coat). I cannot spend the night in a strange man’s rooms.

HELMER. But could we not live here as brother and sister—?
